analysis.one_liner: Creates a new federal property right in databases, letting companies sue and press criminal charges over copying facts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in July 1998 with four Republican cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and was sent to a subcommittee in October, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 1991 Supreme Court ruling held that facts cannot be copyrighted, companies that spend money compiling databases had little legal protection against rivals who copied their work. This bill would create a new federal right in collections of information: anyone who takes a substantial part of a database and harms the owner's actual or potential market could be sued for damages up to triple the loss, face injunctions and impoundment, and even criminal charges carrying up to five years in prison. The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that invest heavily in compiling databases — financial data vendors, legal and commercial publishers, and market-data firms — would gain a new federal cause of action against competitors who reuse their compilations, backed by civil damages, injunctions, and criminal penalties.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a federal cause of action against anyone who extracts or uses a substantial part of a database built with substantial investment, where that use harms the compiler's actual or potential market, with remedies including injunctions, impoundment of copies, damages plus the defendant's profits, and up to triple actual damages.

It adds criminal penalties for willful, commercially motivated violations or violations causing $10,000 or more in yearly loss: up to $250,000 in fines and five years in prison, doubled for repeat offenses.
A new protection lasts up to 15 years after the investment that qualified the information, and all rights are governed exclusively by federal law, preempting inconsistent state rules.

The bill exempts government-produced data from protection and shields nonprofit educational, scientific, research, verification, and news-reporting uses, and reduces or cancels monetary penalties against nonprofit institutions that reasonably believed their use was allowed.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who wants to build a product on facts someone else compiled — competing information services, researchers, journalists, libraries, and startups — would face lawsuit risk, and the public could face higher prices and less reuse of information as compilation becomes more monopolized.
analysis.who_pays_short: Information users, researchers, and data competitors

drawbacks.text: The prohibition covers harm to a compiler's 'potential market,' defined to include any market commonly exploited by similar products — so nearly any competing reuse of a substantial part of a database could trigger liability, going well beyond wholesale piracy and potentially chilling secondary research, comparison services, and product development on top of existing data.

Criminal liability of up to five years in prison for copying data causing $10,000 in losses is a heavy sanction for conduct that, before this bill, was largely lawful under the Supreme Court's Feist decision holding that facts are not copyrightable.

While education, science, research, and news uses are nominally exempt, the exemptions shrink to nothing whenever the use 'harms the actual or potential market' for the database — so the carve-outs depend heavily on litigation outcomes rather than providing genuine safe harbor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to a real problem: wholesale digital copying of an expensive database can destroy the market for it, and after Feist, copyright offered no remedy. But the fix is badly overbroad. By keying liability to harm to 'potential' markets, it converts most competitive reuse of facts into a lawsuit, and it attaches criminal penalties to data copying. The exemptions for education, science, and news are real but erode whenever a court finds market harm, which is precisely the contested case. A narrower bill targeting true wholesale piracy would have addressed the problem at far less cost to researchers, competitors, and the public's access to information.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rod Grams introduced the bill on July 10, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
Four Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
On October 13, 1998, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Technology, Terrorism, and Government.
No further action was taken, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, anyone who reuses and republishes facts — competing data services, researchers, libraries, journalists, and the public that relies on inexpensive access to information — is better off. Database companies lost their chance at a new 15-year federal right in facts backed by civil and criminal penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Information users, researchers, and data competitors

for.name: Sen. Rod Grams
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 10, 1998, and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: Commercial database and market-information industry
for.role: Prospective beneficiary of a new federal database right
for.what_they_did: Backed database-protection legislation following the Feist decision, which had left database investments largely unprotected.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (105th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never voted the bill out; after initial referral it was sent to a subcommittee in October 1998 and no hearing or markup followed before the Congress ended.

against.name: Library, scientific research, and online-user communities
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed database misappropriation bills during this period, arguing they would restrict access to facts and burden research and education.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, but no votes were ever taken in either chamber, so the bill's partisan split on the merits was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would hand companies that compile databases a new federal property right in collections of facts, enforced by lawsuits, treble damages, and criminal penalties. Their gain comes at the public's cost: reduced reuse of information, fewer competing services, and higher prices. Sources: S2, S3.

industries.industry: Securities and commodities exchanges and real-time market data vendors
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes real-time market information from its exemptions and bars its extraction as a substitute for a paid real-time market data service, locking in the exchanges' and licensed vendors' role as paid gatekeepers of market quotes and trades. Sources: S2, S3.

industries.industry: Competing information services and online data businesses
industries.note: New competitors building products on existing compilations would face liability for harm to the compiler's 'potential market,' raising entry costs for rival data services. Their interest runs with the public's interest in cheaper, more accessible information. Sources: S3.

industries.industry: Academic research, libraries, and nonprofit science
industries.note: The bill gives these users express exemptions and reduced penalties, but the exemptions evaporate when a court finds harm to the database's market, leaving them exposed to litigation over ordinary research and news uses. Sources: S2, S3.
